title: An outbreak in southern Sudan
summary: The first documented Sudan virus outbreak spread through communities and health facilities around Nzara and Maridi. The original investigation describes four affected towns and shows why the 1976 story begins in more than one place.
question: How did local movement and hospital care shape the first documented outbreak?
visual: Original 1976 field report and location map
context: UKHSA historical overview and map (OGL v3.0; map revised February 2025)

title: A second outbreak, a new virus
country: Present-day Democratic Republic of the Congo
summary: A separate investigation in the Yambuku area linked many infections to unsafe injections and close contact. The virus later took its name from the nearby Ebola River. This stop distinguishes the Zaire investigation from the Sudan investigation.
question: What can a field investigation establish when laboratory capacity is limited?

title: Outbreaks recur in Central Africa
summary: Several outbreaks in Gabon and neighboring areas showed that emergence was recurring, while the available location evidence varied in precision. The historic geographic database is the starting point for comparing these events without collapsing them into a single point.
question: What does a regional cluster tell us—and what does it leave uncertain?
visual: Historical outbreak maps and GIS collection

title: Kikwit changes the response
summary: The Kikwit outbreak brought renewed attention to surveillance, infection prevention, contact tracing, and community trust. The 2026 anniversary lectures look back on this response, but the outbreak year is 1995, as documented in the original study.
question: How did local clinical and community experience change outbreak practice?
source: Khan et al., Journal of Infectious Diseases, 1999

title: Uganda builds a local response
summary: Uganda's 2000–2001 outbreak illustrates the importance of local surveillance, clinical organization, and community structures. It belongs to the Sudan virus lineage, distinct from Ebola virus disease caused by Ebola virus.
question: Which response capacities can persist after an outbreak ends?
source: Lamunu et al., International Journal of Infectious Diseases, 2004

title: A third major Ebola disease virus
summary: Investigation in western Uganda identified Bundibugyo virus as a distinct cause of Ebola disease. Its identification is important for the timeline: outbreaks caused by different viruses cannot be treated as one uniform biomedical event.
question: Why should a map legend identify the virus, not just the disease name?
source: Wamala et al., Emerging Infectious Diseases, 2010
visual: Discovery study by Towner et al.

title: An epidemic crosses borders
summary: The largest Ebola epidemic to date began in southeastern Guinea and spread through the region. At this scale, dated district maps and changing case reports explain more than a single country marker. This 2014 stop represents one stage of a multi-year epidemic.
question: How does the story change when we zoom from countries to districts and border crossings?

title: An outbreak in Équateur
summary: The 2018 Équateur outbreak was a distinct event in western DRC. The dated June map shows the situation as it was reported during the response, not a final or timeless distribution.
question: What did responders know at this date, and what would later reports add?

title: Eastern DRC: a prolonged response
summary: A separate outbreak in eastern DRC unfolded across North Kivu and Ituri, amid insecurity and displacement. The tour keeps it separate from the Équateur event that began earlier in 2018.
question: How can a map show separate outbreaks that overlap in calendar time?

title: A second geography in 2020
summary: Another Équateur outbreak began while the eastern DRC outbreak was still ongoing. Sequencing and field investigation helped distinguish its origin and transmission from the eastern event.
question: Why is a shared year—or country—not enough to define one outbreak?

title: Guinea sees Ebola again
summary: Guinea reported new Ebola virus disease cases after the West Africa epidemic had ended. The chronology raises questions about persistence, detection, and how a new event should be linked to earlier history without assuming identical transmission pathways.
question: How can the timeline show recurrence without implying uninterrupted spread?
visual: CDC outbreak history and regional overview

title: Sudan virus disease in Uganda
summary: Uganda declared a Sudan virus outbreak in September 2022. The 2022 map is a dated situation snapshot; the WHO event page records the outbreak's conclusion in January 2023.
question: How do a map's data date and the outbreak's end date differ?
visual: ERCC map, data as of 12 November 2022 (CC BY 4.0)

title: Another Sudan virus outbreak
summary: A separate Sudan virus outbreak was declared in Uganda in January 2025 and declared over in April. It is not the same event as the 2025 Ebola virus outbreak in DRC.
question: How can a timeline keep nearby but biologically distinct events clear?
visual: WHO event report and district list

title: The Bulape outbreak
summary: DRC declared an Ebola virus outbreak in the Bulape health zone in September 2025. The map link shows an October response snapshot; the CDC chronology records the outbreak's December conclusion.
question: What changes between a response snapshot and a final event summary?

title: 2026 is still being written
country: Democratic Republic of the Congo and reported international cases
summary: The 2026 Bundibugyo virus outbreak remains ongoing. WHO's 20 November report describes sustained transmission in DRC and reported cases beyond it. The map tour ends with a dated source, not a final total or a claim that the story has closed.
question: What is known as of 17 November 2026, and what may change next?
source: WHO Disease Outbreak News, 20 November 2026; data as of 17 November
